title: A Flesh-Eating Parasite Returns to the U.S. After 60 Years, Threatening the Cattle Industry
summary: For the first time in nearly six decades, a gruesome parasite has resurfaced on U.S. soil. The New World screwworm fly — whose larvae, or maggots, burrow into open wounds and eat living tissue — was confirmed in a 3-week-old calf in La Pryor, Texas, about 100 miles from the Mexican border. The discovery has put ranchers and agriculture officials on high alert. The screwworm is no ordinary fly. Unlike most maggots that feed on dead flesh, these larvae attack healthy animals, including livestock, wildlife, and occasionally humans. A single female fly can lay hundreds of eggs in a wound as small as a tick bite. If untreated, an infestation can be fatal. The U.S. cattle industry, valued at $113 billion, is particularly vulnerable. Texas alone is home to $17 billion worth of cattle. The fly was an annual scourge from the 1930s until the 1960s, when the U.S. launched an ingenious eradication program: breeding billions of sterile male flies and dropping them from planes to mate with wild females, causing the population to collapse. It worked — the pest was declared eliminated in 1966. So why is it back? Experts point to climate change. Warmer temperatures are expanding the fly's tropical habitat northward, and cold snaps that once killed them off are becoming rarer. The fly was detected in Mexico in late 2024 after years of containment in Panama. Since then, it has sickened over 171,700 animals and 2,000 people across Central America and Mexico, with 10 human deaths, according to the CDC. U.S. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins closed border entries to livestock in May 2025, a move she says delayed the fly's arrival by a year. Texas has now imposed a 12-mile quarantine zone around the infected ranch. Animals cannot leave without inspection. Ranchers fear the fly could spread among wild deer, as it did briefly in the Florida Keys in 2016. Officials stress that the fly does not infest food and is unlikely to affect beef prices. But for cattle producers, the threat is real — and the race is on to stop a full-blown resurgence.
why_it_matters: This outbreak shows how climate change can resurrect old pests, threatening food supply and the economy. It demonstrates the importance of scientific methods like sterile flies and rapid quarantine to protect animal and human health.

background_read: The New World screwworm (Cochliomyia hominivorax) is a parasitic fly whose larvae feed on living tissue; it was once a major agricultural pest in the southern U.S. before being wiped out through a landmark scientific effort.

In the 1950s, U.S. Department of Agriculture entomologists Edward Knipling and Raymond Bushland developed the sterile insect technique: mass-rearing flies, sterilizing males with radiation, and releasing them to mate with wild females, causing the population to collapse.

The fly remained endemic in parts of South America and the Caribbean, but a containment barrier has been maintained in Panama (the central American country that acts as a buffer zone) to prevent northern spread.

Since late 2024, outbreaks have surged across Central America and Mexico, driven by warmer temperatures linked to climate change that allow the fly to survive farther north and through milder winters.
In 2016, a small outbreak occurred in the Florida Keys but was quickly contained using sterile fly releases, showing that the technique still works if applied rapidly.

perspectives.description: The quick imposition of a quarantine and the proven sterile insect technique offer hope that the pest can be controlled again. The method is environmentally friendly compared to chemical spraying.

Ranchers face potential economic disaster if the fly spreads into wild deer populations, making eradication harder. Climate change means such reintroductions may become more common, and border closures may only delay the inevitable.

The situation illustrates the interconnectedness of climate, animal health, and global trade. The sterile insect technique is a celebrated scientific achievement, but it requires sustained funding and cross-border cooperation to remain effective.

The U.S. may need to re-establish a permanent barrier in Mexico or develop new monitoring methods. Increased surveillance, public awareness, and investment in parasite research will be critical to prevent a full-blown resurgence in a warming world.
